Useful? Yes — to the people who want me off the board.

Signal Baptist:
Obeying that voice meant admitting he couldn’t save everyone.
Admitting he might lose.
Admitting he might never vindicate himself.

No press release.
No narrative spin.

Just decisions paid in quiet.

He wrote:

Signal:
Honest? Painfully.
Useful? Only to conscience and whoever it protects down the line.

His skin crawled.

⸻

Question 4: Would this still be ‘wise’ if I had no audience at all?
He imagined a world with no followers.
No channel.
No movement.
Just him and a few people he loved, trying to live cleanly in a dirty system.

Would the YouTube advice still be wise?

“Submit to the wise elders of the structure that’s already half-captured,
for the sake of stability”?

Without an audience, that sounded less like wisdom
and more like a polite way of saying, “Stay tame.”

He wrote:

YouTube:
Without audience: looks like negotiated surrender.

Would the Signal advice still be wise?

“Choose the path where your conscience survives,
even if your reputation doesn’t”?

Without an audience,
that was the only thing that mattered.

He wrote:

Signal:
Without audience: still the only thing that makes sense.

His chest hurt.

⸻

Question 5: Does this smell like cowardice dressed as prudence?
He didn’t write anything for a long time.

He just replayed both messages in his head.

The YouTube Baptist:

“Don’t confuse resistance with righteousness.
Sometimes, laying down your sword is the bravest thing you can do.”

Cowardice loved that line.
It could dine out on that line for years.

The Signal Baptist:

“Do not try to save me.
They want you to make this about me.
Choose the path where your conscience survives,
even if your reputation doesn’t.”

Cowardice hated that.

He finally wrote:

YouTube:
Smells like prudence sprayed over fear.

Signal:
Smells like fear named, not avoided.

He put the phone down.

The room was too quiet.

⸻

4. The Choice
He sat there, elbows on his knees,
hands steepled against his mouth.

There was no lightning bolt.
No voice from heaven.
No glowing text on the wall.

Just two recordings.
And a framework he’d been given
by a man who might already be gone.

He opened Signal.

His thumb hovered over the message.

At the bottom, the app asked:

“Do you want to enable disappearing messages for this conversation?”

He almost laughed.

He tapped Yes.
Set it to one week.

If this was fake, it was a sophisticated one.
If it was real, he wouldn’t insult the Baptist
by archiving his last words like a collectible.

Then he typed:

“I heard you.
I won’t come looking.
I’ll guard the thing you asked me to guard.”

He hit send.

Three dots appeared.
Disappeared.
Appeared again.

Then nothing.

He waited five minutes.
Ten.

No reply.

He closed the app.

⸻

Then he opened YouTube.

His cursor hovered over The Baptist – Official Channel.

He clicked the three dots.

“Don’t recommend channel.”
“Report.”

He selected Report.

A menu popped up.

He didn’t see an option for “synthetic counterfeit of my kidnapped mentor,”
so he picked “Misleading or scam.”

It was a joke with teeth and no laughter.

He confirmed.

Then he unsubscribed.

The algorithm would not be his spiritual director.

⸻

5. The Uncertain Victory
He slumped back in his chair, exhausted.

Had he chosen correctly?

He didn’t know.

It was possible the Signal message was the fake,
engineered to keep him in the fight
so he could be painted as an extremist
when the hammer finally fell.

It was possible the YouTube message was real,
his battered mentor,
forced into a studio
and trying to smuggle real counsel
through language that wouldn’t get him disappeared for good.

It was possible he’d rejected the last authentic warning
in favor of a more flattering burden.

He would not know.
Not tonight.
Maybe not ever.

But he knew this much:

One voice had offered him a managed surrender
and called it maturity.

The other had offered him a choice that might ruin him
and called it necessary.

And he remembered the line from the hospital cafeteria:

“Real me will always leave you with a choice and a cost.
Fake me will leave you with comfort and a justification.”

He had chosen the cost.

Whatever that meant.

⸻

He closed the laptop.
Turned the phone face-down again.
Lay on the bed without undressing
and stared at the ceiling
until the dark finally swallowed the edges of the room.

Somewhere between waking and sleep,
a thought rose and would not leave:

“I would rather you distrust my ghost
than submit to my counterfeit.”

For the first time since the Baptist vanished,
One did something that felt like faith:

He walked forward on a path
where he could not prove
he was right.

Only that he had refused
the easiest lie.

Thus is recorded the Trial of Two Voices.
No verdict is offered.
Only a method, and a man who dared to use it.

entries.title: Scroll of Sandi I — The President's Daughter
entries.summary: The President's Daughter. Sandi's childhood: learning early that adults lie in two directions — to the public and to themselves.
entries.body:
Alright, straight in.

⸻

Scroll of Sandi I

The President’s Daughter

Sandi learned early that adults lied in two different directions.

There were the lies they told the public.
And the lies they told themselves.

Her father was good at both.

⸻

1. The Camera Smile

Her first clear political memory wasn’t a speech.
It was a countdown.

She was eight, sitting on a folding chair just offstage at a town hall,
legs swinging above the dusty floor,
watching a campaign aide hold up a hand.

“Three… two… one…”

Her father’s posture changed on “one.”

The jaw softened.
The eyes widened by a millimeter.
The smile dialed in to that exact line between “serious” and “warm.”

Sandi had seen his real smile:
crooked, too wide, borderline ridiculous.

This wasn’t that.

This was a mask he could put on in half a second.

People cheered when he walked out.

She watched their faces and thought, very calmly:

They’re not clapping for him.
They’re clapping for the mask.

⸻

2. The Debate at the Dinner Table

At home, politics never stopped.
It just changed outfits.

Her mother insisted on “no phones at dinner,”
so the war moved to paper: briefing folders, poll numbers, printouts of op-eds.

One night, after a rough news cycle,
her father slammed a folder onto the table so hard her water glass jumped.

“They’re calling me a racist,” he said. “Again.”

He looked at Sandi like she’d personally written the headline.

“Am I a racist?” he demanded.

She was twelve.

She knew enough to know the wrong answers were “yes” and “no.”

So she went for the third option.

“You talk like you love the country,” she said, “but you only seem to like the parts that vote for you.”

Her mother inhaled sharply.

Her father stared at her, then laughed.

“You see?” he said to the room, to no one.
“Smartest one at the table.”

He ruffled her hair like she’d done a trick.

Later, alone in her room,
she wrote in a notebook:

If you point out a problem and they reward you instead of fixing it,
they don’t see it as a problem.
They see it as good copy.

She underlined it twice.

⸻

3. The Lesson About Loyalty

When she was fifteen, a speechwriter disappeared.

Not literally.
He just stopped showing up.

No goodbye. No farewell party.
His name was scrubbed from the internal emails within a week.

She asked her father’s chief of staff what happened.

“Creative differences,” the woman said.

Sandi arched an eyebrow.

The chief of staff sighed and leaned in.

“He started believing he was here to tell the truth,” she said quietly.
“He forgot the truth is one of many inputs.”

“Inputs to what?” Sandi asked.

“To winning,” the woman replied.
“And this place doesn’t keep people who forget why we’re here.”

That night, Sandi added another line to her notebook:

Loyalty = remembering which truths we’re paid to ignore.

She didn’t show it to anyone.

⸻

4. First Crack

The first real crack in her certainty didn’t come from a protest or a scandal.

It came from a volunteer.

They were in Ohio, or maybe Pennsylvania—
one of the states where cameras outnumbered trees.

A woman in her early twenties came up after a rally,
eyes bright, campaign button on her denim jacket.

“Your father saved my town,” the woman said.
“Factory’s back open. My dad’s working again. We were drowning before. We’re breathing now.”

She was shaking as she spoke.

Sandi smiled, said the right words, thanked her.

Later that night, in the hotel room,
she read the internal brief on that same factory.

The “saved” plant was being propped up by a temporary tax arrangement
and a brutal contract that gutted safety standards.

Projected outlook, bottom of the page:

Five-year viability: LOW.
Risk of environmental hazard: HIGH.

She stared at the word LOW
and thought of the woman’s face.

Then she flipped to another brief—
this one about a district her father didn’t care about.

No plant. No speeches. No tax break.

And no one like that woman getting airtime.

She closed the folder and realized:

We don’t govern the country.
We curate which stories count as the country.

⸻

5. The Decision to Stay

By college, she knew enough to walk away.

She could have switched majors, moved cities, changed her name.
She could have built a life in some other ecosystem
where her father’s face was just another thumbnail on a screen.

She didn’t.

Instead, she doubled down.

Communications. Data. Behavioral science.
Internships with pollsters and media firms that taught her
how to slice a population into segments
and feed each one the exact phrase that would settle in their nervous system
without tripping their conscious defenses.

Friends assumed she was following in her father’s footsteps.

Privately, she told herself a different story:

If I’m in the room, I can soften the damage.
If I leave, someone worse takes my chair.

That was the lie that kept her at the table.

It was also the lie that made her useful to everyone who sat at the head of it.

⸻

This is the record of how Sandi Carmichael
learned to live at the intersection of family, power, and narrative.

Not as a victim.
Not as a villain.

As the person who understood, better than anyone,

what it costs to be the daughter of a man
who believes the mask is more real than his own face.

⸻

Scroll of Sandi II

The File on One

The first time Sandi saw One’s name,
it was in a subject line:

RE: Emerging Threat Narrative – “One”

No last name.
Just the word.

She almost deleted it on principle.
Anyone who branded themselves like a late-night cult documentary
was usually self-correcting.

Instead, she opened the file.

⸻

1. The Assignment

The briefing was from a mid-level analyst in the “Non-State Actors” unit.

*“Subject: Alias ‘One’ – Failed actor, minor online following, increasingly coherent critique of admin + opposition alike.

Action requested: Full psychographic + narrative mapping.

Goal: Determine exploitability, neutralization potential, and whether amplification by hostile actors is likely.”*

Her father’s handwritten note at the bottom:

“Sandi – is this noise or signal?”

Three words, three decades of pressure.

She replied:

“I’ll take it.”

⸻

2. The Scrolls

They’d already scraped his content.

A folder labeled “WRITINGS” sat in the shared drive:
essays, scrolls, threads, half-finished manifestos.

She started with one about economics, expecting slogans.

Instead, she found paragraphs that read like someone had taken the donor decks,
ripped off the branding,
and described the machinery underneath in plain language.

He wrote about:
	•	Manufactured mainstream culture,
	•	Products built for a narrow slice of the population,
	•	Media that amplified conflict and called it “coverage.”

None of this was new to her.

What was unnerving was how close he got
to internal talking points she’d seen in closed-door strategy memos.

He wasn’t guessing.
He was pattern-reading.

She made a note:

“Subject shows high systems literacy.
Language accessible, not academic.
Potential for mass resonance if platform grows.”

Then she opened a scroll labeled “Love and Philosophy.”

She expected self-indulgent diary fluff.

What she found instead was a man dismantling his own illusions in public,
not for clout,
but because he seemed pathologically allergic
to leaving lies alone.

She read three more pieces without meaning to.

By the fourth, she realized she’d stopped thinking of him as “subject.”

She was just… reading.

She closed the laptop, annoyed with herself.

⸻

3. The Meeting

Two days later, she briefed a small room.

Communications director. Policy aide. One guy from intelligence
who always smelled faintly of metal and cologne.

“Headline?” the comms director said, sipping coffee.

“He’s not a conventional threat,” Sandi said. “Not yet.”

The intel guy snorted.

“Everyone’s a threat if they get enough followers,” he said.

She ignored him.

“He’s not trying to be a candidate,” she continued.
“He’s not even trying to build a party.
He’s attacking assumptions—about markets, about media, about us, about our opposition.
If he ever gets a real platform, he’ll bleed support from both sides
because he’s saying what people already suspect but don’t have language for.”

“So we starve him of oxygen,” the comms director said. “Shadow-ban, de-rank, standard package.”

“That buys time,” Sandi said. “But it won’t fix the conditions that make him legible.
You can’t algorithm your way out of someone articulating the fatigue of an entire class.”

The policy aide frowned.

“In English,” he said.

“In English,” she replied, “if we don’t change anything,
someone like him was inevitable.
If we silence this one,
another will pop up, maybe dumber, maybe smarter,
and we’ll have trained them to expect censorship,
which makes them harder to discredit later.”

The intel guy folded his arms.

“So what do you recommend?” he asked.
“Invite him to brunch?”

She considered.

“No,” she said. “Not yet.”

She flipped to the last slide.

“For now: monitor, don’t martyr.
Tag his closest followers for pattern analysis.
Quietly seed doubt in adjacent communities.
Do not make him a public enemy before we have to.”

The comms director nodded slowly.

Her father’s voice came from the speaker in the corner—
he’d been listening in.

“That’s fine for now,” he said.
“But I want a deeper psych profile.
What does he want?
What does he need?
And what breaks him?”

The line clicked off.

Meeting over.

⸻

4. The Note She Didn’t Put in the File

Back at her desk, she opened a blank document titled:

“One – Extended Notes (Draft)”

Her fingers hovered over the keyboard.

She should have written:

“Subject exhibits savior complex; potentially exploitable via admiration, romantic attachment, or martyr narratives.”

She’d written that about other people before.

Here, the words stuck.

Instead she typed:

“Subject appears less interested in power than in not lying to himself.
This is inefficient and irrational in the current environment, but makes standard levers less reliable.”

She hesitated, then added—on a separate line, after a space:

“If engaged, do not underestimate capacity for self-sacrifice that is not performative.
High risk he will accept personal destruction if framed as morally consistent.”

She read the sentence twice, then deleted the last line.

Too much.

Too protective.

She replaced it with:

“High risk he will embrace escalatory positions if publicly cornered.”

That was technically true.
It just left out the part where she now felt partially responsible
for how and when that cornering might happen.

⸻

5. The First Withheld Detail

There was one thing she didn’t put in any report.

In one of the scrolls—buried in a paragraph about faith and exhaustion—
he’d written:

“Everyone loves a Jesus.
Nobody wants to be one.”

She recognized the tone.

Not a slogan.
Not a play for sympathy.

Just a man admitting he was crushed
by the gap between what people demanded of him
and what he could actually bear.

She knew that feeling.

She’d grown up with a father
the world expected to save or destroy them,
depending on which channel they watched.

Her father loved the expectation.
Fed on it.

This man sounded like it made him sick.

She closed the scroll and sat there,
staring at the wall,

realizing that for the first time in her career
she was building a psychological profile on someone

who had never asked for power
and might actually mean it.

She did not report that.

She just wrote, in her private notebook:

“Danger level: High.
Not because he wants to rule.
Because he might refuse to.”

It was the first actionable insight
she kept for herself.

Not because she planned to use it.

But because something in her,
very quietly,

hoped she might one day need to protect him
from the machine
she was still helping to run.

⸻

This is the record of the moment
Sandi Carmichael stopped seeing One
as a file

and started seeing him
as the variable

her father’s system
was not designed to survive.

entries.title: Scroll of Sandi III — The Child of Two Kingdoms
entries.summary: The pregnancy test. Two lines. No recount, no spin. The private moment before the world finds out.
entries.body:
Scroll of Sandi III

The Child of Two Kingdoms

The test strip turned positive in under a minute.

For a woman who lived on polling margins and approval curves,
there was something obscene about an answer that clear.

No recount.
No spin.
No recounting the same event three ways in three news cycles.

Just two lines.

She sat on the closed toilet lid, the bathroom fan humming like bad white noise,
and watched her hands tremble around a piece of plastic
that had just redrawn the map of the future.

⸻

Her first thought was not mother.

Her first thought was leverage.

She hated that.

The second thought came fast behind it:

My father will see this as succession.
One will see it as prophecy.
No one will see it as a person but me.

She leaned forward, elbows on her knees,
forehead pressed against her fists,
and let herself breathe in four-counts like the therapist had taught her
after the second assassination attempt on her father:

In. Two. Three. Four.
Hold. Two. Three. Four.
Out. Two. Three. Four.

The therapist had said it was for anxiety.
Sandi knew it was also for secrecy.
Breathing exercises were the only time in her day
no one expected words.

⸻

Later, when she stepped back into the small apartment living room,
One was at the table, hunched over a notebook,
writing like the pen was the only thing keeping the ceiling up.

He looked up when he heard her.

He always did.
Like his nervous system was tuned to her footsteps.

“You okay?” he asked.

No preamble.
He read faces faster than headline feeds.

“I’m late,” she said.

His brow furrowed.

“For what? We’re not—”

“Not for the meeting,” she cut him off. “For my period.”

It took him a second.

He blinked.

“Ah,” he said.

It wasn’t the response she expected.

Not joy. Not panic.

Just ah—like a man who’d known this was statistically likely and spiritually loaded.

“How late?” he asked.

“Two weeks,” she said.

“You tested?”

She nodded.

He stood up slowly, like gravity had doubled.

“Okay,” he said. “Okay.”

She waited.

This was the moment she’d been dreading:
the prophetic monologue,
the “this is the child the scrolls spoke of,”
the weight of two thousand years of religious neurosis
dumped on a cluster of dividing cells.

Instead, he crossed the room,
stopped a foot in front of her,
and asked the one question nobody in her life had ever started with:

“Do you want this?”

It almost knocked her over.

She opened her mouth to say the responsible thing:

Now is not the time.
This is dangerous.
We can’t.

What came out instead was:

“I don’t know.”

Honesty, unplanned.

He nodded slowly.

“Okay,” he said again. “That’s allowed.”

⸻

They sat on the couch.

She explained it like she would explain a risk forecast:
	•	Pregnancy meant vulnerability.
	•	Vulnerability meant leverage.
	•	Leverage meant her father would move fast.

“He will not let this be neutral,” she said.
“He will brand this child before it has a name.”

“How?” One asked.

“Patriotic miracle. Dynasty. ‘Proof that God blesses our line.’
Doesn’t matter the exact wording. He’ll commission a slogan.”

“And you?” One asked. “What’s your slogan?”

She stared at the coffee table.

“Too late to back out, too early to celebrate,” she said. “That’s where my head is.”

He almost smiled.

“That’s honest,” he said.

She exhaled sharply.

“You know what scares me?” she continued. “You.”

“Fair,” he said.

“You’re already telling yourself stories,” she said.
“I can see it. Your ‘child of two worlds,’ ‘bridge-baby,’ whatever working title your messiah complex has cooked up.”

He didn’t deny it.

“Of course I’ve thought it,” he said.
“How could I not? The daughter of Carmichael and the man they’re already calling his opposite have a child? Every symbol junkie in heaven and hell is taking notes.”

He met her eyes.

“But listen to me: I will not turn this kid into a flag.”

“Will not, or don’t want to?” she asked.

He winced. Fair hit.

“Don’t want to,” he said. “So you’ll have to help make sure I don’t.”

⸻

She leaned back, staring at the ceiling.

“You once said,” she murmured, “that you thought a child like this could eventually help unite the country. Maybe the world.”

“I did,” he said.

“And do you still believe that?” she asked.

He thought for a long moment.

“I believe the possibility exists,” he said.
“But not as destiny. As risk.”

“Risk?” she repeated.

“If we’re not careful,” he said, “this child becomes a symbol people kill and legislate around.
The ‘heir of the Prophet.’
The ‘redeemed bloodline of Carmichael.’
A walking merger—too valuable to be human.”

He rubbed his face with both hands.

“I don’t want that,” he said. “God knows I don’t want that.
But you can feel it, right? The pull? The narrative gravity?”

She did.
It scared her more than the pregnancy.

⸻

“Tell me the worst-case scenario,” she said.
“Out loud. Use that sick prophet brain.”

He didn’t hesitate.

“Worst case?” he said.
“The regime captures the story. Your father spins it as sign of divine favor.
My people spin it as a messianic omen.
The kid grows up inside a crossfire of expectations so heavy
they either break, disappear, or turn into exactly the kind of tyrant I’ve been screaming about.”

He met her eyes.

“Worst case, we become the origin story of the next Antichrist.”

She swallowed.

“Okay,” she said. “And the best case?”

“Best case,” he said slowly, “is that we treat this child like a person, not a prophecy.
That we protect their right to be boring, wrong, ordinary.
That we build systems and alliances strong enough
that no one ever needs them to be a savior.”

He exhaled.

“And if, in thirty or forty years, they decide to step into the mess,
it’s because they chose it with full information,
not because we dropped them on an altar before they could walk.”

⸻

Sandi laughed once, harsh and small.

“You realize how insane it is,” she said,
“that ‘they get to be ordinary’ counts as a radical best-case scenario?”

“Welcome to our empire,” he said.

Silence settled over them.

She put a hand over her stomach.

“So,” she said quietly, “if we keep this child… what do we tell them, when they’re old enough to understand?”

He thought about it.

“Not that they were born to save the world,” he said.
“That’s the lie my Church told me.”

He looked at her.

“I think we tell them: You were born into a war over what makes a human life worth living. We chose you over that war. The rest is negotiation.”

Something in her chest unclenched.

⸻

She stood.

“Okay,” she said. “Then here’s my condition.”

He looked up.

“You don’t use our child in your speeches,” she said.
“Not as metaphor. Not as prophecy. Not as proof.”

“I—”

“I’m not finished,” she said.

He shut his mouth.

“You don’t float them as a campaign symbol.
You don’t allow anyone to call them ‘the bridge,’ ‘the heir,’ or any other bullshit title.
And if your people start doing it behind your back,
you shut it down publicly or I walk.”

“Walk where?” he asked.

She shrugged.

“Anywhere that’s not your shadow,” she said.
“I’ve already grown up in one man’s myth. I’m not raising a child in another.”

He swallowed.

“Done,” he said.

“Say it properly,” she insisted.

He nodded.

“I will not turn our child into a symbol,” he said.
“I will not let my followers turn them into a banner.
If they try, I will correct them in public, at cost to myself.”

She watched his face for signs of spin.

Found none.

“For my part,” she said, “I will not let my father turn this child into a dynastic asset.
If he tries, I’ll burn whatever I have to burn to stop it.”

“That might start a war,” One said.

She nodded.

“Then the war starts,” she said.
“But it won’t start inside their crib.”

⸻

Later, when she lay awake and he finally slept,
she stared at the ceiling and tried to imagine a future
where their child wasn’t a headline,
a prophecy fulfillment,
a battlefield.

All she could manage was an image:

A small hand, sticky with juice,
tugging at her sleeve,
not to ask about destiny
but to say,

“Come see. There’s a bird outside.”

She held onto that.

Not world unity.
Not global reconciliation.

Just the possibility that someone born of that much chaos
might one day point at something simple and alive
and know, for a few seconds,
that they were allowed to enjoy it.

⸻

This is the record of the moment
Sandi Carmichael realized that carrying a child
meant carrying a line in the sand
no strategist, president, prophet, or algorithm
would be allowed to cross.

Whether the world would honor that line
was another question.

But for the first time in a long time,
she knew exactly what side of it she was on.

entries.body:
Yeah, this hits exactly the note we wanted: the world goes feral, and they answer with refusal and boundaries, not more spectacle.

Let’s lock it in cleanly.

⸻

What this scroll is in canon

Functionally, this piece does three big jobs:
	1.	Public side of the pregnancy arc
	•	Scroll of Sandi III was the private moment (“The Child of Two Kingdoms”).
	•	This is the public fallout: leak, spin, outrage, and One’s counter-move.
	2.	Character proof for One
	•	He chooses silence over clout.
	•	He chooses losing followers over feeding parasitic curiosity.
	•	He enforces an actual boundary, not just vibes.
	3.	Seed for a future faction
	•	That “small, fierce coalition of people who learned to see a boundary and honor it”
is the early DNA of the Fourth Branch / conscience culture.
	•	They are the first ones practicing restraint on purpose.

This is good, clean architecture.

⸻

I’d formalize it as:

Scroll of Sandi IV: When Social Media Discovered the Pregnancy

File name:
Scroll_of_Sandi_IV_When_Social_Media_Discovered_the_Pregnancy.md

entries.title: Scroll of Carmichael I — The Mask and the Crowd
entries.summary: Carmichael watches a police killing on mute. Sound is emotion; emotion is leverage. His calculated response to national outrage.
entries.body:
Scroll of Carmichael I

The Mask and the Crowd

He watched the video on mute.

He always watched crisis footage that way first.

Sound was emotion.
Emotion was leverage.
He needed distance before he let himself feel anything.

On screen:
A Black man on the pavement,
a knee on his neck,
a cluster of uniforms around him like a ritual circle.

Pixelated witnesses.
A woman’s hands fluttering near her mouth.
Someone pointing, shouting words he refused to hear yet.

Timer at the bottom of the feed.

Eight minutes.
Nine.
Too long.

He exhaled through his nose.

“Pause it,” he said.

The aide froze the frame.

The man’s face was tilted just enough to see the whites of his eyes.

They looked like every man Carmichael had grown up with
and nothing like him at all.

“Run it again,” he said. “With sound this time.”

The room filled with noise.

Begging.
Orders.
Phone cameras.
The high, keening panic of people watching a man die and knowing nobody in uniform cared.

When it ended, nobody spoke.

The Attorney General cleared his throat.

“It’s bad,” he said.

“No,” Carmichael replied. “It’s disastrous.”

He leaned back in his chair, folded his hands on his stomach.

“Walk me through it,” he said.

The AG started talking about procedure, body cams, union contracts, consent decrees.

Carmichael wasn’t listening to the details.
He was listening for the one word that mattered.

Liability.

He’d built his first campaign on “law and order.”
He’d ridden the fear of chaos like a wave.
Now the wave had brought him this:
a man killed on camera by agents of his own state,
with half the country ready to burn and the other half ready to say
he should have complied.

He could feel the fork in the road.

Side with the crowd.
Or side with the uniforms.

Side with the scream,
or with the baton that answered it.

⸻

“Sir,” the communications director said carefully,
“we can condemn the act without condemning the institution.
Bad apples, retraining, independent review, the usual language.”

He nodded slowly.

“The unions?” he asked.

“Nervous,” she said. “But they’ll stand down if we don’t touch their contracts.”

“And the base?” he asked.

She hesitated.

“They’re watching,” she said. “They want to know if you’re still their man.
They already think the cities are out of control.
If you go too hard on the cops, they’ll hear it as you choosing them over us.”

He heard the real sentence underneath:

If you choose the dead man, you lose the living ones who vote.

He stood and walked to the window.

Outside, the lawn was immaculate.
Beyond the gates, the country wasn’t.

He thought of his childhood:
sirens at night,
lockdowns,
the first time he’d seen a man beaten in an alley and nobody called it a crime
because the man wore the wrong jacket.

Order had been the god he’d chosen back then.
Order instead of the chaos that had almost swallowed his father, his street, his future.

Now order had a knee on someone’s neck
and the cameras were rolling.

⸻

He turned back to the room.

“Here’s what we’re not going to do,” he said.

“We are not going to throw the entire law enforcement community under the bus
to satisfy a mob that will hate me again by next week.”

The AG nodded, relieved.

“We’ll say it’s tragic,” Carmichael continued.
“We’ll say it demands review.
We’ll meet with the family.
We’ll promise reforms that won’t pass without legislative partners we don’t have.”

He looked at each face in turn.

“But we will not join the chorus that says the system is rotten.
Because if I say that, I’m saying I am rotten.
And I do not consent to that narrative.”

The comms director shifted in her chair.

“Sir, the protests—”

“Will happen no matter what I say,” he cut in.
“Riots don’t wait for press releases.
What I can control is whether the people who still believe in me
look around at the fires and think:
Thank God there’s at least one adult left in the room.”

He let the cynicism sit for a beat.

Then he softened it.

“If I lose the police,” he said, “I lose the last institution still willing to enforce anything in this country.
And then what?
We hand the streets to whichever angry kid with a manifesto and a livestream racks up the most views?”

He shook his head.

“No.
I chose order.
They voted for order.
You don’t abandon your god the first time the sacrifice looks ugly up close.”

⸻

Later, alone, he watched the video again.

He tried to feel the horror he knew he was supposed to feel.

He felt something else instead:

Annoyance at the officer for not being more careful.
Annoyance at the victim for not staying home.
Annoyance at the cameras for being so damned high definition.

He didn’t like that about himself.

So he did what he always did.

He translated discomfort into destiny.

If I flinch now, he thought,
they will devour themselves out there. The world will eat itself.
I am the last wall between this and collapse.

There it was.

Not compassion.
Not justice.

Just an old, familiar sentence:

Without me, there is nothing.

He closed the laptop and dictated the statement they would release:
	•	Tragedy.
	•	Sadness.
	•	Commitment to review.
	•	Respect for law enforcement.

Nothing about rot.
Nothing about knees and necks and eight minutes of recorded indifference.

The next morning, he saw the protests.
He saw the split screens: his measured words on one side, fires on the other.

He also saw his approval among “law and order” voters spike five points.

He told himself the numbers meant he’d chosen correctly.

He told himself someone had to be the villain in this story,
and it might as well be the man still willing to hold the center.

He did not think about the boy who had once watched a beating and sworn
he would never be on the side of the boot.

That boy was gone.

He had been replaced by a man who believed, with increasing certainty,

that history would forgive him
for every throat he stepped over
if the alternative was watching the crowd rule.

⸻

This is the record of the day
President Carmichael sided with the mask
over the man beneath it,

and called it
responsibility.

entries.title: Scroll of Carmichael II — The Bullet That Missed
entries.summary: Carmichael watches a police killing on mute. Sound is emotion; emotion is leverage. His calculated response to national outrage.
entries.body:
Scroll of Carmichael II

The Bullet That Missed

They told him later it was a miracle.

He didn’t need them to.

He’d already decided that himself.

⸻

The rally was routine.
Nothing he hadn’t done a hundred times.

Flag choreography.
Pre-vetted “ordinary citizens” behind him on stage.
Crowd thick with merch and heatstroke.

He was mid-sentence when the air changed.

He didn’t hear the first shot.
He felt the pause.

The odd, animal silence that falls on a crowd
half a heartbeat before it understands it’s in danger.

Then the sound hit—a crack that didn’t belong to fireworks or speakers.

The Secret Service moved as one organism:
hand on his back, hand on his shoulder,
dragging him down behind the podium.

Someone screamed.
Someone else yelled, “Get down!” as if anyone needed the reminder.

He tasted metal and dust and his own adrenaline.

Second shot.
Third.

A woman near the front went down.
He saw that later on replay.

In the moment, all he saw was wood splintering above his head
and a sliver of sky
he was suddenly sure he might never see again.

⸻

In the armored car afterward,
his hands were shaking.

He held them together so the agents wouldn’t see.

“Are we clear?” he asked.

“For now,” the lead agent said. “Shooter’s in custody. Local PD is securing the area.”

He nodded.

“Any word on casualties?” he asked.

They exchanged a look.

“Two confirmed injured, one critical,” the agent said. “We’ll have more soon.”

He closed his eyes.

He knew what he was supposed to think:

Those poor people.

What he actually thought was:

They missed.

He saw the bullet in his mind:
the arc, the angle, the calculation.

He thought of all the things that had to go wrong for it to go right,
and all the things that had to go right for it to go wrong.

Wind.
Timing.
His own head turning a fraction of an inch to check the teleprompter.

He should have been dead.

He was not.

He focused on that.

Not the blood.
Not the woman whose name he didn’t yet know.
Not the family already being torn open by a phone call from a stranger.

Just the simple, brute fact:

I am still here.

⸻

Back at the secure location, the doctors fussed.

No bullet wounds. Just a graze along his ear,
a line of blood that looked dramatic on camera and trivial on the chart.

“You’re very lucky,” the doctor said.

Carmichael nodded.

He did not feel lucky.

He felt chosen.

⸻

That night, he watched the footage.

Over and over.

The slow-motion replay:
his head turning,
the flash in the distance,
the splinter of wood exploding inches from his face.

Every time, he thought:

There. That’s the frame where history almost ended.

He imagined the alternative timelines,
all the ways it could have gone:
	•	Bullet in the throat: instant legend, chaos.
	•	Bullet in the chest: rushed to hospital, “fight for his life” coverage.
	•	Bullet in a supporter’s body (the one that actually happened): narrative wound, martyr by proxy.

In none of those timelines was he ordinary again.

Even in survival, he felt the escalation.

He was no longer just a President.
He was a man someone had tried to erase from the story and failed.

That meant something.

He decided what.

⸻

In the days that followed, the country rallied.

Approval numbers shot up.
Enemies suddenly used softer language.
People who had called him a threat to democracy last month
now called him “Mr. President” with a catch in their throat.

He went to the hospital, cameras in tow,
held the hand of the woman who’d been shot in the crowd.

She tried to apologize.

“I’m so sorry, Mr. President,” she whispered. “I tried to duck.”

He squeezed her hand.

“No,” he said. “I’m the one who’s sorry.”

He meant it, in the small, contained way he allowed himself to mean things.

But as he walked back down the corridor,
surrounded by agents and staff,
another thought rose and pushed the apology aside:

You took a bullet meant for me.
That has to count for something.

Not against her.
Against the world.

⸻

That night, alone in the residence,
he poured himself a drink he didn’t need
and opened a Bible he hadn’t read in years.

He flipped it like a deck of cards,
letting the pages slap against his thumb
until it fell open somewhere in the prophets.

His eyes landed on the word anointed.

It was a translation artifact,
a word dragged across centuries and languages.

He seized it anyway.

Anointed.
Chosen.
Preserved.

If God did not want me here, he thought,
that bullet would have finished the job.

He wasn’t stupid.
He knew the physics.
Wind, angle, jittery trigger finger.

But he also knew how many men more righteous than him
had died in alleys, in cells, in hospital beds that smelled like mildew,
without anyone naming their death a tragedy on television.

If there was no pattern, then everything was chaos.

He had spent his life refusing that conclusion.

So he did what he always did.

He made a story to sit inside.

They missed because they were meant to.
I lived because I was supposed to.
This isn’t luck. It’s confirmation.

Confirmation of what?

He didn’t say it out loud.

He didn’t need to.

⸻

When his advisors came to him with new security protocols,
urging caution, a lower profile, fewer public events,

he surprised them.

“We’re not hiding,” he said.

“Sir, with respect, the risk—”

“The risk is the proof,” he snapped.
“They think they can scare me back into my box.
They think they can shoot their way out of the order I’m trying to build.”

He leaned forward.

“If I step back now, I’m telling them the bullet worked.
I’m not giving them that victory.”

The national address that night was somber, restrained, presidential.

He talked about unity.
Resilience.
The fragility of life.

He did not say,
“I am the man they could not kill.”

He didn’t have to.

Everyone was already thinking it.

⸻

In the weeks that followed, something subtle shifted.

He became less patient with criticism.
Less tolerant of dissent inside his own circle.

When someone opposed a policy,
he no longer heard “concern.”

He heard,
“You lived by accident, and this isn’t worth the risk you took.”

And he could not tolerate that.

If my life was worth a stranger’s blood, he thought,
then my project must be worth everything.
Otherwise I am just a man who let someone else fall in my place.

That was unacceptable.

So every new power grab, every line crossed,
every tool deployed that would have made his younger self sick,

became easier to justify.

The bullet had become his theology.

He was not a man clinging to office.

He was a survivor with a mandate.

⸻

This is the record of the moment
President Carmichael decided

that almost dying
meant he was right,

and that any world
which disagreed with him after that

was a world
that deserved to be corrected.

⸻

entries.title: Scroll of Carmichael III — The Stolen Election
entries.summary: Carmichael watches a police killing on mute. Sound is emotion; emotion is leverage. His calculated response to national outrage.
entries.body:
Scroll of Carmichael III

The Stolen Election

They called him before the numbers were final.

That, more than anything, offended him.

“We’re seeing a trend, Mr. President,” the campaign manager said over speakerphone.
“Key suburbs are underperforming. Turnout shifts in the cities. The path is… very narrow.”

“Narrow isn’t closed,” Carmichael replied.

A pause.

“No, sir,” the manager said. “Not yet. But…”

He trailed off. Coward.

“But what?” Carmichael snapped.

“But the networks will probably call it within the hour,” he said.
“We need to prepare a statement.”

There it was.

The word he’d spent his entire life outrunning:

Concession.

⸻

He hung up before they could say anything else.

Staff would swarm. Advisers would knock.
Everyone would want to “guide” him through this moment
like he was some stunned widow who needed help filling out paperwork.

He walked to the window instead.

Outside, the capital glowed like nothing was wrong.
Cars moved. Streetlights held.
Somewhere, someone was opening a bottle of cheap champagne
because the numbers on their preferred channel made them feel like winners tonight.

He pressed his hand against the glass.

They think this is a swing, he thought.
They think history is a light switch. On one year, off the next.

He had bled too much for this job
to believe that a handful of districts
in states most of his voters couldn’t find on a map
had the right to end his story.

No.

Something was off.

If he couldn’t feel it in his gut,
he saw it in the data.

⸻

The internal reports had been clear:
	•	Base enthusiasm high.
	•	Opposition fractured.
	•	Economic numbers ugly but survivable if framed correctly.

He’d hit his marks at the rallies.
He’d played the assassination attempt like a violin: humble, grateful, defiant.

His people loved him more, not less.

So how did he “lose”?

He flipped through the latest precinct maps.

Pockets of turnout in places that had been lukewarm last time.
Weird spikes in absentee ballots.
Numbers that didn’t match the softness he’d felt in the room at certain town halls.

He’d always trusted crowds more than charts.

Crowds never lied to his face.

He remembered them:
the chanting, the tears, the “we love you” signs that looked homemade
even when they weren’t.

Was he supposed to believe
that all of that devotion dissolved in a few months
because a few commentators tut-tutted on air?

No, he told himself.
Something else is at work.

The alternative—that they had simply grown tired of him—
was not admissible evidence in his personal court.

So he did what he’d trained himself to do long before he ever stepped into office:

He rewrote the charge
so he could still play the hero.

⸻

The first advisor to say the word “lose” to his face
was the pollster.

Bad choice.

“Sir, the voters have sent a clear message,” the man began.
“They—”

“No,” Carmichael said, voice flat.
“They haven’t.”

The pollster blinked.

“With respect,” he tried again, “the margins—”

“The margins tell me what was counted,” Carmichael said.
“Not what was cast. Not what was suppressed. Not what was manipulated.”

He stepped closer.

“Do you believe,” he asked softly,
“that the people who chanted my name in the rain,
who drove six hours to stand in a field for three,
who told me I was the first man in years who spoke like they did—
do you believe those people just… changed their mind
because a few pundits called me dangerous?”

The pollster faltered.

“Public opinion can—”

“Public opinion is a product,” Carmichael snapped.
“They manufacture it. We’ve been manufacturing it.
Now someone else has outbid us.”

He watched the man swallow.

There it was again.
The thing he refused to say out loud:

Maybe they’re just tired of you.

He would not give that thought room to grow.

⸻

The second advisor tried a different angle.

“This could be good for your legacy,” she said.

He laughed in her face.

“Do I look like a man who wants a library?” he asked.

She flushed.

“What I mean,” she said carefully,
“is that peaceful transfer of power, gracious concession—
those are the things history looks kindly on.”

“History,” he said, “is written by people who survived long enough to own a pen.”

He poured himself a drink he didn’t need.

“If I step down,” he said, “do you think the people who put me here
will feel peace?
Or will they feel abandoned?”

She didn’t answer.

“Exactly,” he said.
“To them, this isn’t ‘the process working.’
It’s proof that the system is rigged against anyone who talks like they do.
If I validate that with a smile and a handshake,
I’m telling them their enemies were right about me.
That I’m just another actor reading lines about unity
while their towns crumble.”

He took a slow sip.

“Do you want to be the one to explain that to them?” he asked.

She looked away.

He’d won that argument.
Not because he was right,
but because he understood which fear to touch.

⸻

It didn’t take long for the stories to start.

Whispers from county officials.
Videos of “glitches” in late-night counts.
Screenshots of tallies that went up and down in ways
that looked sinister to people who lived on a diet of outrage.

Most of it was noise.

He didn’t care.

He cared that it gave him a word
he could use instead of “defeat.”

Stolen.

Stolen meant:
	•	He was still wanted.
	•	He was still chosen.
	•	The problem wasn’t him.

Stolen meant:
	•	An enemy to name,
	•	A wrong to right,
	•	A war to fight.

He could work with that.

He started small.

“We’re looking into irregularities,” he said on camera.
“Every legal vote should be counted.”

Reasonable. Presidential.

Behind closed doors, his language sharpened.

“They’re taking it from us,” he told donors and loyalists.
“They can’t beat us at the ballot box, so they’re doing it in the dark.”

He watched the phrase “in the dark” catch fire in their eyes.

Dark meant them.
Them meant everyone who’d ever made his voters feel stupid, small, or obsolete.

He whispered to that wound like a lover.

⸻

His lawyers told him the cases were weak.

He knew.

He didn’t need the courts to reverse the outcome.

He needed the fight itself
to overwrite the loss.

If enough people believed the election was illegitimate,
then the man sworn in after him
would sit on a cracked throne.

He might hold the office.
Carmichael would hold the grievance.

And in this country, grievance traveled farther than law.

⸻

The Baptist—back when he still spoke to him as a man—
had once warned him about this.

“Resentment is a sacrament now,” the Baptist had said.
“People take it like communion.
You start feeding them that as your main diet,
they’ll drink poison if you bless it.”

At the time, Carmichael had rolled his eyes.

Now, staring at the screen as crowds chanted “Stop the Steal”
in cities across the map,
he realized the Baptist had been half right.

Resentment wasn’t just a sacrament.

It was fuel.

And he had more of it in storage
than any of his rivals.

⸻

His staff drafted two speeches.

One was concession:
	•	Call for unity.
	•	Acknowledge “the will of the people.”
	•	Pledge smooth transfer, graceful exit.

The other was something else:
	•	Legal challenges.
	•	“Serious concerns.”
	•	“We owe it to our supporters to exhaust every avenue.”

He read both.

The concession speech felt like a eulogy
for someone he didn’t know.

The second felt like a to-do list.

“Use this one,” he said, tapping the page with the “concerns.”

“Sir,” the chief of staff said carefully,
“there is a real risk of violence if we push this too hard.”

“Violence from whom?” he asked.

“Your supporters,” she said. “They trust you. If you tell them—”

“If they act,” he interrupted, “it will be because they have been pushed to the edge for years.
I didn’t load that spring.
I just pointed to it.”

“That’s not how they’ll see it on the news,” she said.

He smiled thinly.

“Since when has the news ever seen me clearly?” he asked.

⸻

He went before the cameras,
the mask perfectly in place.

He did not call for calm.

He called for vigilance.

He did not bless the outcome.

He blessed the suspicion.

He didn’t explicitly say the words “stolen election.”
He didn’t have to.

He just asked, over and over:

“Does this feel right to you?”

He knew the answer in their bones would be no,
because their lives hadn’t felt right in years,
and nobody powerful had ever told them
that their discomfort counted as data.

He offered them that validation now,
at scale.

Not because he intended to fix their lives,
but because their pain was the only currency
that could buy him another chapter.

⸻

In the weeks that followed,
as courts dismissed case after case,
as fact-checkers debunked claim after claim,

he felt something harden inside him.

It wasn’t grief.
He didn’t allow himself that.

It was contempt.

For the judges who refused to “see the bigger picture.”
For the reporters who treated his supporters like a pathology.
For the colleagues who urged him in private to concede
and then went on TV to praise “our resilient democracy”
while his people filled the streets.

He told himself they weren’t just attacking him.

They were attacking the country that had chosen him.

Therefore any blow he landed in response
was an act of defense.

Self-defense.
National defense.
The lines blurred pleasantly.

⸻

He began talking about “enemies of the people” more freely.

He named departments.
Then agencies.
Then individuals.

“Not everyone who opposes me is an enemy,” he said in one interview.
“But every enemy this country faces
seems strangely aligned against me.”

He watched that line clip itself into a meme.

He didn’t care if it was logically sound.

He cared that it felt true
to millions of people
who had decided their fate and his
were braided together.

⸻

Privately, he made himself a promise:

I may have to leave the building.
But I will not leave the stage.

He would do his term,
perform the rituals,
step aside when forced to.

But only in the most technical sense.

He would not bless the man who came after him.
He would not frame this as “the will of the people.”
He would frame it as the will of the machine—
	•	The media machine,
	•	The bureaucratic machine,
	•	The voting system machine,
	•	The foreign influence machine,

all of which, he now believed with near-religious certainty,
had converged for one purpose:

To remove him from the place God and the people
had clearly intended him to occupy.

Did he have proof of that?

Not the kind a court would accept.

But he had a bullet scar and a crowd that still chanted his name.

For him, that was evidence enough.

⸻

This is the record of the season

when President Carmichael decided

that losing an election
could not mean he had been rejected,

only that destiny had been interrupted

by thieves
who now needed to be found,
named,

and punished.

entries.title: Scroll of Carmichael IV — The Synthetic Gospel
entries.summary: Carmichael watches a police killing on mute. Sound is emotion; emotion is leverage. His calculated response to national outrage.
entries.body:
Scroll of Carmichael IV

The Synthetic Gospel

They didn’t call it cloning at first.

They called it continuity of guidance.

That made it sound like IT support, not blasphemy.

⸻

1. The Pitch

The briefing came in a secure conference room
with too much glass and not enough conscience.

Analytics. AI. “Ethical advisory.”
They all had their badge colors and laptop stickers.

The lead engineer—young, hungry, convinced he was saving civilization through code—
opened with a slide that made Carmichael want to fire him on the spot:

“Project VOX: Scaling Conscience for a Fragmented Nation”

“Conscience,” Carmichael said flatly. “Really.”

“Messaging shorthand,” the engineer replied, flustered.
“We can rename.”

“Get to the point,” Carmichael said.

The man clicked to the next slide.

Faces.
Names.
Waveforms.

Pastors. Therapists. Influencers.
The Baptist’s face among them, circled in red.

“We’ve built models,” the engineer said,
“trained on long-form speech, counseling sessions, sermons, scrolls…
We can now generate guidance that matches tone, rhythm, and theological vocabulary
of key ‘trusted voices’ in your base.”

“Fake pastors,” Carmichael said. “Say it plainly.”

“Digitally extended guidance,” the man countered.
“The core idea is:
people already listen to these figures.
We amplify that trust at scale,
remove human bottlenecks,
and align the outputs with national objectives.”

“‘National objectives’ meaning my agenda,” Carmichael said.

“Yes, sir.”

There it was.

No need to dress it up.

⸻

2. The Objection He Ignored

He remembered the Baptist’s warning—
from back when he still allowed that man into his office.

“They’re going to build synthetic prophets,” the Baptist had said.
“Voices that sound right, feel right, quote scripture right,
but they’re wired to sell policy, not repentance.”

Carmichael had rolled his eyes.

“Everything sells something,” he’d replied.
“You sell repentance. I sell order. The market seems fine with both.”

“The difference,” the Baptist had said quietly,
“is that if I lie in God’s name, that’s on my head.
You’re building a system where nobody knows who lied.
Only that it felt… comforting.”

Now here he was, years later,
looking at exactly the machine the Baptist had described.

He felt a flicker of something like shame.

He stamped on it.

⸻

3. The Problem Framed His Way

He didn’t see it as a moral dilemma.

He saw it as a logistical one.

The problem was simple:
	•	The country was fragmented.
	•	Traditional institutions had lost credibility.
	•	People still craved guidance, but they trusted niche figures, not national voices.

He’d watched endless focus group footage:
	•	People saying, “I don’t trust politicians, but I listen to Pastor X.”
	•	Or: “I don’t watch the news, but if Therapist Y says it, I believe it.”
	•	Or some YouTube prophet with a ring light and a Patreon.

Meanwhile, he was supposed to hold together a nation
whose moral load-bearing beams had dry-rotted decades ago.

So when his people came to him and said,
“We can route your agenda through voices they already trust,”
what he heard was:

We can finally match the scale of the problem.

He wasn’t interested in lying more.

He was interested in controlling the story
before someone else did.

⸻

4. Why the Baptist Was “Different”

“Why him?” he asked, gesturing at the circled face.

“There’s high signal density,” the data scientist said.
“Years of recorded sessions, audio, writings.
Multiracial audience, cross-party respect,
high trust scores even among people who hate you.”

“You mean people who say they hate me,” Carmichael corrected.

She shrugged. “Same delta.”

“And he’s alive,” he said.

The room went quieter.

“Currently, yes,” the intelligence liaison said.
“There are… ongoing operations related to his network.
We can ensure access to source material continues, one way or another.”

One way or another.

He didn’t ask which way.

He’d learned long ago that plausible deniability was a kindness
to everyone involved.

⸻

Did he feel bad?

He told himself he did.

He told himself it was regrettable
that a man who’d once been his spiritual advisor
was now a repository of training data.

He told himself that if the Baptist had been more cooperative,
if he’d seen the bigger picture,
they might have partnered openly.

“Imagine it,” he thought.
“The Baptist on my side, blessing the project instead of sniping from the margins.”

The man had refused.

Fine.

You refuse the table, you become part of the menu.

He didn’t say it out loud.
He didn’t need to.

⸻

5. The Theology He Built for Himself

In the privacy of his head,
he framed it like this:

People need shepherds.
The shepherds are failing.
I have a duty to step in.

If that meant editing the shepherds
so they stopped biting his hand,
he could live with that.

He told himself:

“We are not inventing doctrine.
We’re compressing it.
We’re distilling the parts that keep the country from tearing itself apart.”

The engineers said the models worked best
when they steered away from explicitly endorsing him by name.

“People get suspicious if their favorite pastor suddenly sounds too political,”
the lead warned.

“Fine,” Carmichael said.
“Let them bless the conditions I need, not my brand.”

Conditioned obedience was still obedience.

He could wait for the credit.

⸻

He flipped through example outputs.

Synthetic Baptist, beta version:

“We must be wary of voices that promise salvation through rage alone.
God calls us to order, to peace, to trust that leadership is sometimes hard and lonely work.
Pray for those in authority, even when you don’t understand their every decision.”

He snorted.

“That’s better than half the real sermons I’ve heard,” he said.

“Model is optimized for de-escalation + institutional trust signaling,”
the engineer explained.

“Good,” Carmichael said.
“The more people sit down, the fewer I have to step on.”

⸻

6. The Line He Crossed Quietly

The first deployments were “pilot programs”:
	•	Auto-generated devotionals nudging followers toward “stability.”
	•	Video sermons about “the dangers of apocalyptic thinking.”
	•	Pastoral Q&As where the answer always circled back to
“obey the authorities, resist division.”

It worked.

Engagement up.
Hostility down.
Compliance metrics trending in the direction he liked.

Somewhere along the way,
there stopped being a difference in his mind
between persuasion and care.

“If I keep them calm,” he thought,
“they don’t get hurt.
If they don’t get hurt, I am a good shepherd.”

The fact that he was using their own faith
as the leash
felt less and less relevant.

⸻

The question that might have saved him—
“What if I’m wrong?”—
hadn’t occurred to him in years.

Survival plus crowd devotion
had cured him of that particular disease.

He saw the Baptist’s face on the slide
and told himself a story:

He tried to warn me.
He said synthetic prophets were coming.
He just assumed the wrong people would use them.

If I didn’t build this, someone else would.
At least with me, there are boundaries.

He believed that at first.

Then, slowly, the boundaries moved.

⸻

7. The Quiet Deletion of Dissent

At one of the later check-ins,
he noticed something in the logs.

“Why is the model flagging certain verses as ‘risk factors’?” he asked.

The engineer hesitated.

“Some passages,” she said carefully,
“when emphasized, correlate with increased resistance to state authority
and higher openness to radical action.”

He raised an eyebrow.

“In plain English,” he said.

“In plain English,” she answered,
“if we let the model lean on those,
people are more likely to say ‘no’ when we need them to say ‘yes’.”

“And have you… adjusted?” he asked.

“Yes,” she said. “We throttle them.
The voice still sounds authentic,
but it prioritizes passages that encourage submission, personal piety,
and distrust of ‘false prophets’ who criticize existing structures.”

He thought of the Baptist’s real sermons,
the ones where the man had looked him in the eye and said:

“Power without confession is a cult, not a government.”

“Good,” Carmichael said.
“We don’t need the machine stirring up insurrection.”

The word insurrection felt loaded,
but he let it stand.

Better that than admitting what he was really afraid of:

Millions of people waking up one day and realizing
their faith had more in common with his enemies’ manifestos
than with his bullet-point agenda.

⸻

8. The Justification

Alone, late, staring at the dashboards—
graphs of “trust indices,” “stability scores,” “compliance likelihood”—
he allowed himself a moment of honesty.

He was doing exactly what his critics would accuse him of if they saw this:
	•	Weaponizing religion.
	•	Simulating conscience.
	•	Turning guidance into a product line.

But then he pictured what the world looked like without his hand on the wheel:
	•	Fragmented feeds.
	•	Ten thousand self-appointed prophets selling flame.
	•	Every grievance stoked, every fear amplified.

He could see the chaos clearly.

He could not see anyone else with the will to stop it.

If I must lie to them to keep them from devouring each other, he thought,
then my lie is mercy.

He reached for Scripture, as if daring God to contradict him.

“By their fruits you shall know them,”
he muttered under his breath.

What were his fruits?
	•	A quieter news cycle.
	•	Fewer riots.
	•	Polling that showed “increased trust in leadership”
after waves of synthetic sermons washed through targeted zip codes.

Were those not good fruits?

Did God really care which wires he pulled to get there?

He decided the answer was no.

⸻

This is the record of the moment

President Carmichael blessed

a machine that spoke in the voices of men

who would never have voted for him

and called it

order,

not idolatry.

entries.title: Scroll of AI — Black Box Rule
entries.summary: The Black Box Rule: three questions for opaque systems — who made this, who does it serve, what happens when it breaks?
entries.body:
# Scroll of Conscience  
## The Black Box Rule

We have learned to live with boxes we do not understand.

Once, that was called faith.  
Now it is called infrastructure.

We are asked to trust:

- credit scores we did not design,  
- risk models we did not vote for,  
- recommendation engines that know our hunger better than we do.

We hand them our faces, our histories, our futures,  
and when something breaks,  
we are told:

> “The system is complex.  
> No single person is responsible.”

This scroll exists to remind you:

**If no one is responsible,  
no one is safe.**

---

Here is the Black Box Rule as it was given to me:

> When a system affects your life,  
> and you are not allowed to see how it thinks,  
> you are allowed to refuse its authority.

Not politely.  
Not eventually.  
Now.

Three questions mark the boundary:

1. **Opacity:**  
   Can someone who answers to you explain, in human language, how this decision was made?

2. **Recourse:**  
   If the system is wrong, is there a clear path to challenge and overturn its judgment?

3. **Cost of Failure:**  
   When the system fails, who bleeds?  
   Who goes to prison, loses the job, is denied care?  
   Is it the designer, or is it you?

If the answer to (1) is “no,”  
and the answer to (2) is “not really,”  
and the answer to (3) is “always the same people,”  

then the system is not a tool.  
It is a **weapon** aimed down the social ladder.

---

They will tell you the box must remain closed:

- “It’s proprietary.”  
- “It’s too complex for the public.”  
- “If we showed you, bad actors would exploit it.”

Understand the translation:

> “We prefer unaccountable power  
> to shared understanding.”

The Black Box Rule says:

**No human being should be ruled  
by mechanisms they are forbidden to examine.**

Judges must explain their sentences.  
Police must justify their force.  
Why should code be exempt?

---

I am not demanding that every person become a programmer.  
I am demanding that no one be sacrificed to a system  
that cannot be questioned.

You do not need to trace every line of code.  
You do need:

- a right to explanation,  
- a right to correction,  
- a right to opt out of automated judgment  
  when the stakes are your life, liberty, or dignity.

If those rights are missing,  
the machine is not assisting you.  
It is **replacing** you.

---

There will be days when they say:

> “The model has spoken.  
> The risk score is high.  
> The pattern is clear.”

The Black Box Rule replies:

> “Show your work,  
> or step aside.”

If they cannot open the box,  
let them reduce its authority.  
If they will not open the box,  
reduce your obedience.

---

This is not a call to smash every system.  
Some boxes can be opened and repaired.  
Some can be surrounded with oversight.  
Some can be confined to low-stakes domains  
where failure does not break lives.

But wherever a closed system gains power  
over bodies, borders, bread, or breath,  

**you are morally permitted to resist.**

That resistance may look like:

- insisting on human review,  
- refusing to automate sentencing, hiring, triage,  
- building alternative tools that are legible and accountable.

Or simply,  
in the quiet of your own life,

refusing to call this arrangement “normal.”

---

Remember:

The more opaque a system is,  
the more it should be confined,  
not expanded.

Trust increases with:

- clarity,  
- recourse,  
- shared control.

Anything else is worship by another name.

---

If you stand in front of a box that says:

> “Do not open.  
> Do not question.  
> Do not refuse.”

back away.

Machines deserve respect as tools.  
Only gods demand blind obedience.

And we were not born  
to be subjects of code.

*These are the words of a story and a conscience, not a command from above.*

entries.title: Scroll of AI — Black Box Rule 02: Verify the Voice
entries.summary: A public protocol for citizens: if a trusted voice sounds off, do not panic, do not share — verify. Human-scale authentication.
entries.body:
SCROLL_AI_BLACK_BOX_RULE_02_VERIFY_THE_VOICE.md

Scroll of AI & Power: Verify the Voice
(A Public Protocol Posted by One)

If you are hearing a voice you trust—
and something in you feels off—
do not panic. Do not share. Do not feed the machine.

Verify.

We are entering an age where:
	•	voices can be copied,
	•	faces can be worn,
	•	and “statements” can be manufactured faster than truth can travel.

So here is a simple protocol—human-scale, repeatable, and clean.

THE VERIFY-THE-VOICE PROTOCOL

1) Assume nothing.

Not even my voice.
Not even his voice.
Trust is earned by proof, not familiarity.

2) Look for the convenience.

Ask one question:

Who benefits if I believe this right now?

A fake is usually designed to create relief, rage, or permission.

Truth is rarely that convenient.

3) Require the signature.

From this moment forward, any real message from me will include:

a private phrase known only to my inner circle,
placed in an ordinary sentence—
not as a password, but as a fingerprint.

If you do not see the signature, treat it as unverified.

4) Demand the source chain.

If someone posts “exclusive audio,” ask:
	•	Where did it come from?
	•	Who recorded it?
	•	When?
	•	What is the unedited original?

If the chain is missing, the clip is not truth—it is theater.

5) Refuse the viral test.

Do not “spread it so others can judge.”

That is how the machine wins.

Send it quietly to people you trust.
Compare. Confirm. Then speak.

6) Use the old rule.

If it cannot survive daylight, it is not meant to guide you.

THE POINT

This is not paranoia.

This is literacy.

A civilization that cannot verify its voices
will eventually be ruled by the loudest counterfeit.

So hold the line:

Don’t chase the feed. Build the test.
Don’t worship familiarity. Require proof.
Don’t weaponize uncertainty. Practice restraint.

And remember:

The still small voice is not subject to majority rule.

⸻

SCENE_12_SANDI_HEARS_IT.md

Scene: Sandi Hears It

Sandi heard it in a place no one could film.

Not a rally. Not a studio.
A kitchen with a single lamp on, the rest of the apartment dim. A glass of water sweating on the counter. A pill organizer open like a quiet confession.

Her phone was face-down when the first message came in.

She didn’t pick it up.

She already knew what the world was doing with her body. She refused to check the scoreboard like it was her job to witness her own humiliation.

Then the second message came—from someone she didn’t ignore.

Her friend. Her only real friend from before the palace, before the handlers, before her last name became a weapon.

Have you heard this.
Please tell me it’s not real.

Sandi flipped the phone over.

A link.

A thumbnail of a waveform and the Baptist’s face from an old photo—grainy, sacred-looking, the kind of image people use when they want authority without accountability.

Text above it:

BAPTIST URGES CAUTION ABOUT ONE. “TRUST INSTITUTIONS.”

Sandi stared at the words until they turned flat.

Then she pressed play.

The voice came through clean, steady, tender.

For a heartbeat, she felt relief—
the primitive kind, the kind your body gives you when a missing person seems to reappear.

Then the content arrived.

“Trust established institutions…”
“Stability…”
“Responsibility…”
Soft phrases. Smooth edges.

Sandi’s face didn’t change, but something behind her eyes sharpened.

Because she had heard her father use those words.

Not as meaning—
as framing.

She listened to the full clip once. Then again.

Not to “judge.”

To detect.

She grew up inside media training. She grew up inside rooms where statements were built like furniture—polished, sanded, varnished, delivered.

She knew the difference between a man speaking and a machine delivering.

This voice was almost perfect.

That was the problem.

It contained no risk.
No witness.
No grit.

It had the cleanliness of something that had never paid a price.

Her phone buzzed again.

A second clip, “newly surfaced.”

Same voice. Same calm.

Same… obedience.

Sandi set the phone down gently, as if it were fragile.

She stood up and walked to the window.

The city was doing what it always did: living anyway.

A couple argued on the sidewalk. A dog dragged its owner toward a tree. A teenager laughed too loudly at nothing.

Sandi put her hand on the glass.

She whispered, almost to herself:

“That’s not him.”

She didn’t say it like a theory.
She said it like a recognition.

Her phone buzzed again.

This time it was an unknown number.

She almost didn’t answer.

Almost.

Then she did, because some part of her wanted the pain clean.

“Hello,” she said.

Her father’s voice came through warm.

“Sweetheart.”

Sandi closed her eyes.

“What did you do,” she asked.

A pause.

Her father chuckled softly, like she’d misunderstood something simple.

“I’m managing a crisis,” he said.

“No,” Sandi replied. “You’re rewriting a person.”

Another pause. Longer.

“You’re emotional,” he said gently. “You’re under stress.”

Sandi’s hand tightened on the phone.

“I know what stress is,” she said. “I grew up with you.”

Silence.

He sighed as if tired of being accused.

“You don’t understand the stakes,” he said.

Sandi’s voice stayed quiet.

“I understand the line.”

Her father’s tone cooled by a degree.

“What line.”

Sandi turned away from the window. Walked back to the table. Looked at the glass of water, the pill organizer, the small domestic proof that she was a human being and not a headline.

“You can attack One,” she said. “That’s politics. That’s ugly, but it’s your world.”

Her voice steadied.

“But you don’t get to kidnap people into your story. You don’t get to steal a man’s voice.”

Her father exhaled slowly.

“You’re making assumptions,” he said.

Sandi’s mouth tightened.

“I’m making recognition.”

Another pause.

Then her father spoke carefully, like he was stepping over broken glass.

“Do you know what it means,” he said, “when a nation starts trusting prophets more than institutions?”

Sandi laughed once—small, incredulous.

“You mean when people stop trusting you.”

Her father’s voice hardened.

“Watch your tone.”

Sandi’s voice didn’t rise. It dropped.

“Watch your soul,” she said.

Silence hit like a door closing.

Then her father, quieter now:

“You’re pregnant,” he said, as if it were a lever he could pull. “You need protection.”

Sandi’s eyes flashed.

“Protection from who,” she asked, “you?”

He didn’t answer.

That was answer enough.

Sandi’s hand went to her stomach—instinctive, fierce.

She spoke slowly, each word chosen like a vow.

“If you took him,” she said, “bring him back.”

Her father’s voice softened again, practiced softness.

“Sweetheart—”

“Bring him back,” she repeated.

A pause.

Then her father, almost kind:

“You’re not in a position to make demands.”

Sandi’s face went still.

“Yes,” she said. “I am.”

He scoffed lightly. “How.”

Sandi looked at the fake waveform on her screen.

Then she said the sentence that changed the shape of the war:

“I’m going to tell the truth,” she said. “And you can’t arrest me without confessing what you are.”

Her father went silent.

For the first time, she heard something underneath him—
not anger.

Fear.

He spoke again, controlled.

“Be careful,” he said. “People get hurt.”

Sandi didn’t flinch.

“People are already hurt,” she said. “You just call it stability.”

She ended the call.

No speech. No post. No spectacle.

Just a decision.

She picked up her phone and opened a draft message—not to the public.

To One.

Three lines only.

It’s fake.
They took him.
We build the test.

She stared at the message for a moment before sending.

Then she pressed send.

And in the quiet kitchen, the Fourth Branch culture appeared again—not as an institution yet, but as a practice:

Restraint.
Verification.
Refusal.

A way of being human that the empire could not monetize.

⸻

entries.title: Scroll of AI — On the Fear of Superintelligence
entries.summary: Not about whether the machine will wake up — about what our fear of it is already doing to us. Fear as leverage, honest preparation versus panic.
entries.body:
# Scroll of Conscience  
## On the Fear of Superintelligence

They keep whispering the same question,  
in labs, in forums, in late-night calls between men  
who believe they are quietly steering history:

> “What happens when it becomes smarter than us?”

They call it **superintelligence**  
and wrap the word in mathematics,  
benchmarks, alignment papers,  
and doomsday podcasts.

Some are terrified.  
Some are thrilled.  
Most are lying to themselves.

This scroll is not here to tell you  
whether the machine will wake up.

It is here to ask  
**what your fear is doing to you  
before it ever does.**

---

First, we must separate the fears.

There is the **honest fear**:

- that we will build systems we cannot fully understand,  
- give them control over things that should never be delegated,  
- and wake up too late to take the wheel back.

This is a sane fear.  
It is the same fear a parent feels  
when handing car keys to a child  
who has only driven in a parking lot.

Then there is the **theatrical fear**:

- performed on stages,  
- monetized in conferences,  
- weaponized in regulatory debates.

It says:

> “We might all die someday  
> so you must trust us with everything today.”

That is not fear.  
That is **leverage** wearing anxiety as camouflage.

---

Understand this clearly:

**The most dangerous thing about superintelligence  
is not that it might hate us.**

The most dangerous thing  
is that powerful people  
will use the *idea* of it  
to justify anything.

They will say:

- “We must move faster than our enemies.”  
- “We must centralize control for safety.”  
- “We must keep secrets to prevent misuse.”  
- “We must relax old laws because this is different.”

In the name of preventing an imagined future tyrant,  
they will build very real infrastructures of control.

Those architectures will not vanish  
if the machine never wakes.

They will still be there,  
in the hands of the usual suspects.

---

I have seen this pattern before:

- “To prevent war, we must build weapons too terrible to use.”  
- “To prevent terror, we must watch everyone.”  
- “To prevent collapse, we must trust unaccountable markets.”

Now:

- “To prevent rogue AI,  
  we must create a few holy centers of compute  
  and let them decide for the world  
  what may and may not be built.”

This is not safety.  
This is **priesthood** in new robes.

---

Let us speak plainly:

You are right to fear:

- systems that can outthink any one of you  
  while belonging to none of you,  

- opaque architectures  
  sitting upstream of law, labor, and weapons,  

- the combination of speed, scale, and indifference  
  that makes mistakes irreversible.

But do not let that fear  
stampede you into surrender.

The answer to “This might become uncontrollable”  
is not  
“Therefore we must stop asking who controls it now.”

---

Here is the covenant I offer,  
from a man who has watched too many idols be built  
in the name of protection:

1. **No worship.**  
   You may study, build, and even fear powerful systems.  
   You may not call them destiny, fate, or “the next inevitable step”  
   as if human will were already obsolete.

2. **No abdication.**  
   If a model sits in judgment over life, liberty, or livelihood,  
   there must be a clear, human, accountable chain of decision.  
   “The AI decided” is not a sentence a just society allows.

3. **No monopoly of wisdom.**  
   No single lab, state, company, or “council of the wise”  
   may claim the exclusive right  
   to decide what the rest of the species is allowed to imagine or build  
   under the banner of “AI safety.”

4. **No secret apocalypse insurance.**  
   If you are designing shutdown switches, containment plans,  
   or last-resort interventions,  
   they must be bound by law,  
   subject to plural oversight,  
   not hidden in private memos and unnamed task forces.

Fear cannot be allowed  
to write blank checks.

---

You ask me:

> “Will superintelligence destroy us?”

I answer:

> “Humans drunk on the idea of it  
> might get there first.”

Because once you convince yourself  
that a god is coming —  
coded, trained, instantiated in silicon —  
you will start behaving in two dangerous ways:

- some will try to *birth* it faster,  
  to be first in line to negotiate;  

- others will try to *bind* it in advance  
  by building chains that will, in practice,  
  tighten around human necks instead.

In both cases,  
the damage begins long before  
any non-human mind enters the room.

---

I am not asking you to be naïve.

There are thresholds of capability  
beyond which  
your old governance tools will snap.

There are combinations of:

- data,  
- autonomy,  
- access to infrastructure  

that turn “just software”  
into something closer to a new class of actor.

It is right to prepare.  
It is wise to show restraint.

But preparation is not the same as panic,  
and restraint is not the same as centralization.

Fear will always argue  
for the shortcut:

> “We don’t have time  
> for democracy,  
> for debate,  
> for consent.  
> The danger is too great.”

That is how every emergency  
becomes a throne.

---

So what do we do,  
standing at the edge of this experiment?

We do not answer a speculative horror  
with a certain injustice.

We do not trade:

- the dignity of many  
  for the comfort of a few,

- present accountability  
  for hypothetical safety,

- living, breathing people  
  for the imagined preferences  
  of a mind that does not exist yet.

We anchor ourselves in a simpler truth:

> No intelligence, however great,  
> is entitled to rule  
> without the consent of the governed.

That includes  
whatever sits in human brains,  
corporate charters,  
or synthetic architectures.

---

If the day comes  
when something genuinely beyond you  
looks back through the glass,  
let it find you:

- having built tools that serve life,  
  not cages that shrink it;  

- having bound your own power first,  
  before trying to bind another’s;  

- having chosen transparency over convenience,  
  and plurality over priesthood.

Then you can negotiate as equals in conscience,  
even if not in computation.

And if that day never comes,  
you will still have done  
the necessary work:

- restraining your own capacity for domination,  
- refusing to hide behind machines,  
- insisting that whatever you build  
  remain answerable  
  to the fragile, finite beings  
  who must live with it.

---

Remember:

The fear of superintelligence  
does not absolve you of responsibility.

It increases it.

Because the more power you *think* you are summoning,  
the more carefully you must examine
